entry.summary: This article was automatically translated by Google "Gemini". The author does not guarantee its accuracy or wording.
entry.content:
info

This article was automatically translated by Google "Gemini". The author does not guarantee its accuracy or wording.

While browsing around today, I noticed that OCI's Free Tier terms changed. Looking closer, they actually sent out a notice on June 15 this year.. but I never pay much attention to OCI's emails...

OCI Always Free A1 Resources Before vs. After Update​

Resource Item🔄 Before Aug 2026 Update🚨 After Aug 2026 Update (Latest Policy)💡 Account Restructuring & Ops Impact
Max OCPU per Account4 OCPU2 OCPU (Cut in half)Excess instances will be automatically terminated (Terminate) by the system.
Memory (RAM) per Account24 GB12 GB (Cut in half)Max quota per single VM drops to 12 GB; combined total across multiple VMs cannot exceed this either.
Monthly Free Usage Limit3,000 OCPU hours / month
18,000 GB hours / month		1,500 OCPU hours / month
9,000 GB hours / month		PAYG (Pay-As-You-Go) users usually won't have VMs deleted for exceeding the limit, but overages will be billed directly to the credit card.
Max VM Combination Examples• 1x 4C/24G large VM
• 4x 1C/6G micro VMs		• 1x 2C/12G full-spec VM
• 2x 1C/6G standalone VMs		Resource reshuffle: ditch fragmented tiny VMs and consolidate compute to get the most value.
Free Block Storage (Total Disk)200 GB200 GB (Unchanged)Although disk wasn't shrunk, splitting across 2 VMs leaves very little space per VM—still a storage pain point.
Free Outbound Public Traffic (Network)10 TB / month10 TB / month (Unchanged)Bandwidth allowance remains super generous, great for acting as a high-bandwidth relay or sharing space.

Impact​

Honestly, even though my OCI setup looks super fancy right now—with a WireGuard mesh and all that—the only services I actually use are:

  • Wireguard for BT download - this is to keep copyright trolls off my back
  • V2Ray via 3X-UI - this is for friends still in Chinathe bandit zone Everything else is just flashy fluff that makes no difference if wiped out.

I checked carefully and haven't been charged yet, and it seems PAYG isn't being strictly enforced right now either, though with a trust shift like this it's best not to gamble on a corporation's goodwill.... Better to proactively downgrade myself for peace of mind.

New Plan​

Honestly I haven't thought it through completely yet, but my rough plan is as follows: My current three accounts will probably be split up like this:

Account A A-1 1C6G running the current WireGuard role (basically keeping its current scale and purpose) joined to the mesh A-2 1C6G for running 3X-UI and things provided to friends The nice thing about this is for security settings, only Account A needs ports 80/443 exposed externally, while the other accounts stay open only within the Mesh.

Accounts B & C B 2C12G I don't know what to do with it yet, but join it to the mesh C 2C12G I don't know what to do with it yet, but join it to the mesh

With the specs cut in half, AI workloads that barely couldn't run before definitely can't run now.... so I have even less idea what to use them for.... Still, I'll probably reorganize things first.

Bonus​

Since Watchtower has been acting weird lately, I plan to switch to a systemd timer triggering docker compose up -d to automatically update my Docker images. Once I get that set up, I'll update my wiki with it as well.

entry.title: Long Time No Update, Missed You All
entry.content:
info

This article was automatically translated by Google "Gemini". The author does not guarantee its accuracy or wording.

Ever since I started adjusting how the new Blog/Wiki is presented back in April, I haven't touched any of this for a long time. Partly because I got sucked into vibe coding, and partly because work has been hectic.

Recent Status Report

Even though nobody really cares about what a middle-aged guy has been up to, I still want to jot things down like a diary—organizing what I've been doing lately and what I plan to do next.

Vibe Coding​

To cut to the chase: it failed. Not only did I fail to build anything useful, I even paid for a full year of Gemini AI Pro. Still, there are a few takeaways I want to leave behind.

Simply put, the failure of this vibe coding experiment can't be blamed entirely on Google. Even though plenty of people online say Gemini is trash at coding, blah blah blah, objectively speaking, the main reasons for the failure came down to two things:

  • Not having a clear idea of what I actually wanted to build Strictly speaking, it's because I lack creativity. I came up with a bunch of ideas that seemed promising, only to realize in the end that the return wasn't worth the effort, there wasn't a real need, or someone had already written a great open-source project I could just use directly. That killed my motivation to keep burning brain cells on it.

  • Knowing too little about programming concepts—even when AI wrote a mountain of code, I couldn't read it or tell where problems might arise This issue was glaringly obvious. From structuring a program's framework, planning architecture, choosing a language, and defining variables, to keeping the AI from going off the rails across multiple turns and designing for future maintenance and revisions from the start—all of that was far beyond my ability to plan ahead. In other words, no matter how good AI is at writing code, if the human drafting the blueprint has an empty head, it's still useless (okay, this applies to plenty of other domains too, like governing a country, a company, or a project).

So for now, that whole effort is completely on hold. That said, strictly speaking, if I just ask AI to write simple shell scripts—things I can actually understand—it's still super handy.

Work-Related Stuff​

Office Politics​

Thought I was going to spill something here?? Nope. I'm not dumb enough to leak work details in a place like this. Just making a note for myself: emotionally, this period at work left me with some pretty unpleasant memories, so I'm leaving a footnote.

Slackin' on the Clock​

Strictly speaking, this is about the company issuing me a new laptop. This machine is pretty interesting: a Lenovo ThinkPad P16 Gen 3 with an NVIDIA RTX PRO 1000 GPU and two SSDs. I took advantage of a loophole during the company's Windows installation—one of the SSDs wasn't mounted, formatted, or brought under management—and installed Arch Linux on it for my writing setup. Now I can have a working Arch Linux environment even at the office without relying solely on WSL all the time (though my work Windows still has WSL too).

As for the story of this Arch Linux setup, I might write more about it later if I feel like it—or just skip it if I don't.

New Toy Acquired​

Basically, I picked up a retired company Dell Latitude 5411 on the cheap and brought it home. After thinking about it for a while, I decided to turn it into my very first personal Arch Linux laptop.

Main Time Sink​

Everything above was just trivial stuff over the past few months. What I've really been thinking about and working on lately is the following.

Rebuilding the Home Entertainment Center​

For a long time now, I've wanted to completely overhaul my home gaming setup. Ideally, I'd have a machine in the living room capable of streaming or running games up to a certain performance tier natively, while heavy-hitting PC AAA titles could either be played directly in the study or streamed out to the living room. So I took inventory of all the machines I already have (all old hardware) and started planning the revamp.

NVIDIA SHIELD TV Pro​

This is currently the main set-top box for watching videos in my living room. I once tried installing RetroArch and Moonlight on it, and here's what I found:

  • Moonlight runs, but it depends heavily on a gaming streaming machine running Sunshine.
  • RetroArch runs smoothly up through the SNES (SFC) era, though storage space is a major issue.

Steam Deck​

As my main handheld, I've actually been thinking about switching it to another Steam account, setting up emulators properly, and moving the whole thing along with its dock into the living room to replace our current Switch (since the Switch Joy-Cons are broken... and the screen has cracks too). However, this approach hits a couple of roadblocks:

  • The Steam Deck's emulation capability starts struggling past the PS2 era—though it really is my best living-room console option right now.
  • It's my personal toy, and I really don't want the kids wrecking it.

Dell Latitude 5411​

This machine has zero value for gaming because it has no discrete GPU and only 8GB of RAM—it contributes nothing meaningful to gaming. However, because it exists, it took over the Steam Deck's role as my casual Linux desktop. That's the only reason I can free up the Steam Deck in the first place.

MSI GL73​

This gaming laptop equipped with an NVIDIA RTX 2060 Mobile is currently my best-performing gaming machine, running Windows—the most game-friendly OS.

The Catch​

The vision sounds great, but reality is brutally harsh—I ran into problems before even starting the work.

The biggest issue is that this home entertainment center isn't meant for just me alone. Almost all existing tools and approaches assume one big premise:

Owner of the games = Player = Controller of everything

The moment you have to factor in kids playing too—controlling their playtime and restricting which games they can play—you immediately land on the solution of adding a Steam child account into a Family Group so you can manage kids' playtime and game libraries via Steam's built-in features. As for emulators, since storage on a living-room device is limited, you simply put only curated games on it from the start. That sounds lovely, right? But here's the problem: if the living-room machine is powerful enough on its own and doesn't need streaming, everything is solved—it's just a standalone console. What if you need a beefier streaming host to run games that demand high-end hardware?

Long story short, I tested running games on the Steam Deck via Steam Link over my home network, and "utterly unplayable" doesn't even begin to describe it... Meanwhile, the Moonlight/Sunshine approach has no account isolation whatsoever (since it streams the entire desktop). So if I want to include AAA titles, I'd have to dedicate a streaming host for them, and on top of that figure out how to stream the games I want to play, how to separate accounts and isolate sessions... Things get way too complicated, and I'd need to add more machines to pull it off.

Implementation Progress So Far​

Right now, I've been unifying my bare-metal Arch Linux setups and aligning their configurations closely with the Steam Deck's SteamOS + EmuDeck integration—organizing my previously neglected emulator resources while also paving the way to eventually stop using Windows altogether...

Conclusion​

If I give up on living-room streaming, I could repurpose the Steam Deck into an emulation box plus some kid-friendly / living-room-friendly Steam games. The only catch is I'd effectively lose my handheld, or have to share the console with the kids... Until I buy a new gaming rig, this isn't a bad compromise—assuming the kids' mom doesn't make me kneel on a washboard and dismantle the whole thing for making it too convenient for the kids to play games...

entry.title: Automated Multimedia Setup Adjustments
entry.summary: Adjustments to my current Servarr configuration
entry.content:
info

This article was automatically translated by Google "Gemini". The author does not guarantee its accuracy or wording.

info

This article was reposted from the old site archive.

To fix the issue that had been bothering me for a long time with lidarr's API connecting to Musicbrainz, I made some adjustments to my automated free pirated media setup(automated multimedia collection setup).

Adjustments

Lidarr​

Incident​

The root cause was that Musicbrainz changed its API-related settings, causing lidarr to fail to retrieve metadata from Musicbrainz properly, which basically rendered lidarr useless.

Countermeasure​

Simply put, the ultimate solution was to wait. Once you waited long enough, the lidarr dev team actually released an updated version of lidarr to work with Musicbrainz's new settings (though the text search part is still beyond saving). BUT since everyone couldn't wait earlier, before the dev team fixed it, people started using modified builds or adding mods. As a result, those who used a modified build found that upgrading directly to the new official version didn't work either—which led to the painful ordeal that followed.

The Tortuous Process​

Because this old guy proactively adopted the best solution available at the time(couldn't wait six or seven months and got itchy fingers), after the update I had no choice but to completely wipe the entire lidarr config, then reconfigure everything and re-import the files... Yeah... that process really was long and exhausting...

Differences Between Old and New​

The biggest difference is that the fixed lidarr still cannot use text search like before to search directly by artist name or album name and add new. Instead, you have to go to Musicbrainz first to look up the artist's Artist ID or the album's Release group ID.

Then go into lidarr's add new and use:

lidarr:<artist ID/Release group ID>

And just like before, select the cover that pops up and add it into lidarr.

Subtitles​

Reason​

Nothing special really—just that the author of the ChineseSubtitle plugin I used previously got too busy and abandoned the project...

Replacement​

After looking around, I switched to Bazarr. The setup was just as simple—just spin it up with Docker.

Impressions​

Bazarr is basically part of the *arr family too, so it integrates very well with the rest of my multimedia stack. However, with subtitles, it's like: if you can find them, you find them; if you can't, you can't—just like "whoever gets more votes wins, whoever gets fewer votes loses," a truism that's still basically stating the obvious...

Networking​

Automedia Setup Adjustments​

Originally, based on reference guides, I wrapped the entire automedia stack (including radarr, sonarr, lidarr, jackett...) inside Gluten. However, Gluten's VPN has been acting up lately (honestly, I'm not even sure how long it's been broken). First I noticed jackett + flaresolverr were acting weird, so I moved that pair out of Gluten. Then while fixing lidarr (yep, the one mentioned above...), I found that add new search couldn't connect... After decisively moving lidarr out of Gluten, it worked immediately... So I moved everything in the entire automedia stack out of Gluten except qbittorrent. After all, that matches my ideal setup anyway—only qbittorrent goes through the VPN to stay safe, while the other services don't waste VPN bandwidth... And then I realized the issue mentioned in the reference guides—that they wouldn't be able to talk to each other if not placed together—had disappeared... (probably because I deliberately assigned static IPs to every container in automedia...)

VPN - ERROR [vpn] getting public IP address information:​

Just add PUBLICIP_ENABLED=false under enviroment in docker-compose.yml and it's fixed.

Conclusion

You really shouldn't expect an open-source solution to run forever with the exact same config file without adjustments (even commercial software needs minor tweaks across version updates...). Fortunately, the changes were minor, so it should be good for another few years.

entry.title: UniFi Controller Broke Again (and Again) Because of an AUR MongoDB Upgrade~~~
entry.summary: Chronicles of wrestling with UniFi Controller upgrades
entry.content:
info

This article was automatically translated by Google "Gemini". The author does not guarantee its accuracy or wording.

info

This article is reposted from the old blog archive.

Recently I got a bit diligent about updating my system... and then my UniFi Controller blew up right under a single yay -Syu --noconfirm.

Incident Log

After firing off yay -Syu --noconfirm and letting it run all the way through... the UniFi Controller Web UI became unreachable. Started investigating and found:

  • systemctl status unifi.service reported active and ok, yet netstat -an showed no listening port for UniFi Controller.

  • Checked /var/log/unifi/server.log and saw exit code=62.

  • Checked systemctl status mongodb.service and saw exit code=62 there too; looking into it revealed MongoDB couldn't start normally because the database version was too old.

  • Checked /var/log/mongodb/mongodb.log and confirmed the MongoDB data version was 7.0, while the updated mongodb-bin package in the AUR was version 8.2—too big of a version gap, so it refused to start.

  • Switched to installing the mongodb80-bin package, which allowed upgrading MongoDB's major version to 8.0 via commands.

The frustrating detour part:

  • MongoDB's database upgrade concept:

    • MongoDB cannot skip multiple versions in one jump when upgrading a database (yes, MongoDB's binary version and database version aren't automatically coupled—they're separate and must be upgraded manually).

    • Going from 7.0 to 8.2 requires stepping 7.0 --> 8.0 --> 8.2. Generally a newer version is compatible with the previous version's database, whereas a newer database cannot work with an older binary.

  • The chaotic detour experience:

    • First I removed both the unifi and mongodb-bin packages, installed mongodb80-bin instead, and upgraded the admin database from 7.0 --> 8.0 --> 8.2.

    • Then I removed mongodb80-bin again and reinstalled mongodb-bin and unifi. systemctl status mongodb.service looked fine, and systemctl status unifi.service looked fine too, yet UniFi Controller still wouldn't come up—checking /var/log/unifi/server.log still showed exit code=62.

    • No matter how much I looked around, I still couldn't figure out how to upgrade UniFi's own MongoDB database (this is probably because this old guy hadn't put skill points into the right tree... so I looked completely clueless here).

    • And so I got stuck with the main MongoDB admin database upgraded fine, while UniFi's MongoDB database couldn't be upgraded....

    • Finally I checked UniFi's PKGBUILD file and discovered... its dependency just requires any mongodb....

    • In the end, pairing mongodb80-bin + unifi worked because 8.0 is compatible with a 7.0 database, and it magically came right back to life.....

Key Technical Takeaways

The two main things learned from this incident:

  • MongoDB concepts and upgrades — I still need to look into how to upgrade MongoDB databases other than admin (honestly I couldn't even list the databases).
  • I need to look into how to upgrade UniFi in the future without hitting landmines. I tried running it in Docker before, though I didn't stick with it due to networking issues—maybe it's time to dig that back up.

Following that previous Archlinux crash incident I thought had happened, I got trolled by KDE Plasma yet again....

Tragedy Strikes Again!?

A great man haunted by a scumbag spirit once said, "People keep repeating the same mistakes... good grief!" Yes, once again I got trigger-happy with yay -Syu --noconfirm followed by a bunch of sync commands and sudo reboot. And then my VNC couldn't connect again.... Checked it out and found that my plasma-x11 option had vanished...

The Truth Is Always One!

Yep, the culprit was KDE Plasma... Digging through a bunch of posts, I discovered that starting from Plasma 6.4, the X11 session was removed from the default installation... So I started hunting for a KDE + Wayland remote desktop solution again...

Then, right as I was trying out krdp and getting frustrated with its performance... I discovered:

Turns out you can manually install the X11 session~~~~​

So without hesitation, I slapped the machine with a yay -S plasma-x11-session --noconfirm. And the problem is solved postponed until Plasma 7 comes around.

Ramblings

Although I know the whole community has been shouting that Xorg is too old and pushing to gradually migrate to Wayland.. Right now, in practice, I really haven't found a remote desktop solution that feels more efficient than vnc.. Maybe in the not-too-distant future, I'll switch everything over to moonlight/sunshine, because all the current rdp solutions on Linux feel pretty sluggish to use— nowhere near as smooth as Windows....

entry.title: Finally Ran Into It... Arch Linux Bricked...
entry.summary: Bad luck hitting a crash after an update
entry.content:
info

This article was automatically translated by Google "Gemini". The author does not guarantee its accuracy or wording.

info

This article was migrated from the old blog archive.

Actually, it's not really Arch Linux's fault... (Okay, okay, I know Arch Linux is true love...)

The Crash

I used to see people say that if you use Arch Linux, you need to be mentally prepared for it to randomly die after an update. Having used it for nearly 10 years (Wait!! Am I really that old already? I started using it in 2015...), honestly, I had never once experienced a crash from an update, so I had a hard time understanding why anyone would refuse to update just to avoid breaking things....

Until last week, when I casually hit my remote desktop with a yay -Syu --noconfirm and then discovered... there was no "then". The machine looked powered on, yet remote connections failed. I went into ESXi to check the Console and it was a completely black screen.... It... bricked..

Root Cause

How would I know what the root cause is... I don't even know how to code..

However, I ran the following tests:

  • Installed Manjaro with sddm + KDE plasma - Works normally
  • Installed EndeavourOS with KDE - LiveDVD boots, but black screen after a fresh install
  • Re-install
    • Tried options like linux-6.14, linux-lts-6.12, etc., and it still booted to a black screen after installation and reboot
    • Switched to gdm + KDE Plasma - Works, though inside ESXi only Wayland works normally

And all of these issues also occurred when tested under VMWare Workstation 17 Pro....

Suspected Causes​

  1. sddm does not get along with VMware—aside from Manjaro, anything using sddm gives a black screen on boot
  2. X11 does not get along with gdm—even though using gdm shows a display, trying to log into a plasma-x11 session runs into issues

Based on the two points above, Broadcom forgot to pray to the gods VMware has been disliked by everyone ever since its change of ownership...

Conclusion

My current setup is gdm+KDE Plasma, but because wayland-plasma doesn't support VNC and this machine is mainly used as my VDI, I used systemd to run vncserver@:1.service so the machine starts a plasma-x11 session over VNC on boot. So far it hasn't had any issues, though it looks like I'll eventually have to migrate from ESXi to PVE.

On a side note, this incident didn't affect my other console-only Arch Linux machines, so strictly speaking it doesn't really count as Arch Linux bricking. Great!! My confidence in Arch Linux didn't drop—it actually went up (wait, what??)

entry.title: Novels... I'd Die Without Light Reading...
entry.content:
info

This article was automatically translated by Google "Gemini". The author does not guarantee its accuracy or wording.

info

This article is reposted from the old site archive.

Not having novels to read, just like not having manga to read, is going to kill me.....

Japanese Light Novels

Originally, I always went to MobiNovels (魔筆小說) to grab the Japanese light novel e-books uploaded by the site owner, but later the site owner had a daughter and accidentally lost the site, so for a while I didn't update my own library... Until recently, when I discovered something great.

Tampermonkey - Greasy Fork - Wenku8 Downloader (轻小说文库下载)​

This is truly a blessing, because it can automatically convert novels on Wenku8 (輕小說文庫)—currently the site with the largest free collection—into epub format and pack the illustrations and cover image inside before downloading...

Notes

  • Brave users need to turn off Brave Shields, otherwise the script will be blocked from running
  • For those who want the filenames directly in Traditional Chinese, please click CC開啟 (Enable CC) first—it will convert the filenames to Traditional Chinese
  • Downloading all together merges all volumes into a single file for download
  • If there is a problem downloading any image, it will throw an Error instead of giving you an epub with missing images

Chinese Power-Fantasy Web Novels

Chinese power-fantasy web novels are trickier—basically you have to find websites offering full-book txt downloads. Currently, I go to Free Novel Net (免費小說網) to download the full-book txt files. Because Chinese web novels easily run into millions of words and generally only contain text anyway, I don't expect covers or illustrations...

Converting to epub​

Since I always read on a kindle, I forcibly convert txt files to epub for archiving. Also, since I work in a Linux (penguin) environment most of the time now, the conversion tool naturally has to run on Linux. You ask why not use a web-based converter? Mainly because Chinese web novels have too much text, free online converters can't handle them, and I just want to stay a freeloader..

txt2epub​

txt2epub github - There are many tools with the same name; I picked this one because it can be installed with yay, while most others are installed via pip. On Archlinux, I just run yay -S txt2epub and it's done...

~~Basic syntax

[Kiwi]#> txt2epub -o </path/filename.epub> --author <author Name> --title <book title> --cover-image <filename.jpg> chapter01.txt chapter02.txt chapter03.txt

Notes

  • This thing is purely a CLI command. If you want a GUI, use pip to install another Python txt2epub—I saw a GUI version
  • Make sure the text is unicode before converting, otherwise there will be issues

kaf-cli​

Before this, I used txt2epub for conversion, but found the text formatting of the converted files was a complete mess, so I switched to kaf-cli, which can also be installed directly with yay. The syntax is very similar to txt2epub.

An excerpt of the instructions from GitHub is as follows:

Command-line mode parameters

Usage of kaf-cli:
  -align string
        标题对齐方式: left、center、righ。环境变量KAF_CLI_ALIGN可修改默认值 (default "center")
  -author string
        作者 (default "YSTYLE")
  -bookname string
        书名: 默认为txt文件名
  -bottom string
        段落间距(单位可以为em、px) (default "1em")
  -cover string
        封面图片可为: 本地图片, 和orly。 设置为orly时生成orly风格的封面, 需要连接网络。 (default "cover.png")
  -cover-orly-color string
        orly封面的主题色, 可以为1-16和hex格式的颜色代码, 不填时随机
  -cover-orly-idx int
        orly封面的动物, 可以为0-41, 不填时随机, 具体图案可以查看: https://orly.nanmu.me (default -1)
  -filename string
        txt 文件名
  -font string
        嵌入字体, 之后epub的正文都将使用该字体
  -format string
        书籍格式: all、epub、mobi、azw3。环境变量KAF_CLI_FORMAT可修改默认值 (default "all")
  -indent uint
        段落缩进字数 (default 2)
  -lang string
        设置语言: en,de,fr,it,es,zh,ja,pt,ru,nl。环境变量KAF_CLI_LANG可修改默认值 (default "en")
  -line-height string
        行高(用于设置行间距, 默认为1.5rem)
  -match string
        匹配标题的正则表达式, 不写可以自动识别, 如果没生成章节就参考教程。例: -match 第.{1,8}章 表示第和章字之间可以有1-8个任意文字
  -max uint
        标题最大字数 (default 35)
  -out string
        输出文件名，不需要包含格式后缀
  -tips
        添加本软件教程 (default true)
  -unknow-title string
        未知章节默认名称 (default "章节正文")
  -volume-match string
        卷匹配规则 (default "^第[0-9一二三四五六七八九十零〇百千两 ]+[卷部]")
PS: 在darwin(mac、osx)上-tips参数要设置为false的方法 kaf-cli -filename 小说.txt -tips=0

Command-line mode instructions Convert 全职法师.txt and set the author name to 乱

# windows 10: win + s 搜索powershell 
cd d:/
d:/kaf-cli.exe -author 乱 -filename d:/全职法师.txt

# linux / mac下, 把kaf-cli-linux/kaf-cli-darwin重命名为kaf-cli, 放到用户目录
# 把小说和kaf-cli放到用户目录下,  打开终端执行
cd ~
./kaf-cli -author 乱 -filename ./全职法师.txt

# 如果kaf-cli放到path里了, 或者在aur安装的可以执行:
kaf-cli -author 乱 -filename ~/全职法师.txt

# 命令行的简单模式（功能和拖拽模式一样）
kaf-cli ~/全职法师.txt

Update to kindle

Basically, for Japanese light novels, I just throw them into my light novel library — Calibre-Web — and use Calibre-Web's built-in feature to send books to my Kindle, so there's no problem there. However, I haven't set up a Calibre-Web instance for Chinese web novels yet (maybe later if the collection grows, or I'll put them into my general books Calibre library). Regardless of the future, right now if I want to manually push them to Kindle, I rely on Amazon's official send to kindle, which has a web-based uploader.

Once it's done, you can download it on your Kindle and enjoy reading non-stop...

entry.title: Bought It... Yet Human Desire Is Truly Bottomless...

Having no money while harboring deep desires is truly tormenting.

Desires

TV​

At the end of last year, I finally decided to get a TV for the living room, because I really couldn't stand the whole family cramming into my study to watch movies together on a single 32" monitor... After thinking it over again and again, I bought this cheap 86" TV.

TV BOX​

After using the TV's built-in Google TV for a while, I noticed that videos with external/separate subtitle files easily suffered from subtitle out-of-sync issues and the like. So the beast inside couldn't hold back anymore, and I bought what is currently hailed as the most powerful TV BOX — the Nvidia Shield TV Pro 2019. Yes, even though it's from 2019, it somehow still has the best performance on the market... Makes you wonder whether the hardware was overkill back then or other brands are just being stingy with specs...

Thoughts & Impressions​

  • Damn expensive — It actually cost over 6k NTD. Even the latest Google TV Streamer 4K (a 2024 product) only costs around 3k+ NTD, yet this five-plus-year-old piece of hardware still sells for this much...
  • The SoC is genuinely fast — I looked up the Nvidia Tegra X1+ (the same chip as the Nintendo Switch... roughly 5th-gen i5 level performance). It's about twice as fast as the MediaTek chip in the Google Streamer 4K (though power draw is triple at 15W).
  • 4K AI Upscaling — Actually, this feature was the main reason I bought it, and it's also its biggest selling point. However, in initial use my untrained eyes can't tell a huge difference yet... Plus not every app supports it (for example, Duboku doesn't trigger Upscaling), though maybe I just haven't configured it right—I'll try again soon.
  • Gaming stream — Since I don't use Geforce Now, I can't comment on it, but I have used moonlight to stream my Steam games (Ace Combat 7). It looks pretty decent and pairs smoothly with a Bluetooth controller.

The next step will probably be gradually turning it into part of an entertainment center without messing up Android (besides Emby which I already use, maybe streaming games via moonlight... or running something like an emulator collection).

Gaming Server (Under Consideration)​

Lately I've been stuck in a To be or Not to be state... It started because what I really want is a laptop with a dedicated GPU to run a Linux host (since right now, outside of the Steam Deck's desktop mode, I don't have a physical Linux terminal to use), and I'd really like to set up a penguin machine as a daily driver (a toy that can actually get work done). Considering that buying a brand-new laptop outright doesn't seem as cost-effective as building a new Gaming Server and freeing up the gaming laptop currently filling that role to repurpose it, I dove headfirst into researching desktop builds. Here's what makes it tough:

  • Haven't followed desktop builds and specs in ages — Since 2011, I haven't bought any desktop that wasn't meant to be a server; I switched completely to laptops. My shopping habits also changed from going to Guanghua Digital Plaza to buy parts to browsing PChome, ordering online, and waiting for delivery at home... Going back to DIY feels really unfamiliar now, and I have no mental baseline left.
  • Gap between budget and expectations — My mental model was still stuck in the era when laptops cost more than desktops. After looking around, I have to admit that the PMs behind every laptop spec actually worked hard to balance the configuration... Looking at desktops makes it way too easy to fall into the trap of "just spend a bit more for better specs," only to blow past the budget by the end—yet sticking to the budget leaves specs feeling slightly lacking and hard to swallow. After all that, it feels like only winning the lottery could solve it.... =_=!!

It's gotten to the point where I'm thinking I might as well put that money into stocks instead... That'd probably give a better return... Besides, the moment I turn on my computer, two kids pull chairs up on my left and right, squeezing into my 120cm-wide desk and asking "Daddy, what are you doing..." It really kills any urge to buy one...

entry.summary: Freeloading with WSL on a company PC
entry.content:
info

This article was automatically translated by Google "Gemini". The author does not guarantee its accuracy or wording.

info

This article is reposted from the old blog archive.

After updating qemu, the default WSL kernel turned out to lack TC module support, which set me down the path of no return: compiling my own Linux kernel...

Story

Actually, the story is pretty much what the preface already said (so why am I still rambling?). A few extra details are below:

  • My WSL runs on my company Windows machine, and my Local Administrator privileges were revoked. Plus, since I'm not in an R&D department, getting them back is basically hopeless, meaning I can't update the WSL version via wsl --update.
  • Even if I could run wsl --update, I checked the WSL-Kernel source on GitHub and the default config doesn't have TC or QoS kernel support anyway... (Wait, so my first point above... yeah, it was purely complaining about having no permissions...)
  • The WSL kernel doesn't support dynamically loading modules (in other words, the modporbe command is completely useless in WSL...), so there's no way to load TC/QoS dynamically.

So... this old guy had no choice but to configure and compile the kernel himself to satisfy his needs.

Technical Details

I'll put those in my Wiki (Updated 2026-11-27: WSL Custom Kernel)—feel free to check it out if you're interested.

Reflections

A long, long time ago, back when I used Gentoo, I configured and compiled a Linux kernel (how could you use Gentoo without doing it yourself??), but after that I never bothered doing it manually again (just like long, long ago when I was diligent enough to configure and compile my own FreeBSD kernel, whereas now I just use GENERIC).

Honestly, this hands-on attempt looked intimidating at first, though in practice it wasn't bad at all... You just have to get used to the fact that for a WSL kernel, everything is either enabled or disabled—anything you want to use has to be built-in rather than built as a module. This is basically the same as early FreeBSD kernels, and conceptually different from how mainstream Linux kernels are used today.

And under that model, the hard part—aside from the specific features you know for sure you need (like TC/QoS for this time, plus wireguard support which I use a lot)—is remembering which modules are essential for WSL itself. That's why every guide you see recommends running:

zcat /proc/config.gz > .config

or

cat /proc/config.gz | gunzip > .config

to dump the currently running WSL kernel config as your baseline, and then simply add whatever else you need on top. That approach simplifies away all the parts that would otherwise fry your brain.

Finally... once everything is working properly, WSL is still a blast to use—especially when you're slacking off at the office on a company Windows PC you aren't allowed to wipe, WSL really is the salvation of us wage slaves...

It is already 2025. Although there isn't much to sigh about, I have indeed tweaked a few things recently.

BT over VPN

A colleague was sued by a copyright troll and had to pay a settlement... This incident more or less planted a seed of worry in my heart... So when I saw the introduction related to Gluetun mentioned in Ivon's Blog, I got eager to try it out.

Implementation​

I have updated it to My Wiki (Updated 2026-11-27: Automated Media Binge-Watching Wiki)! Interested folks can refer to my approach.

Thoughts​

It seems to work for now, but qBittorrent's efficiency doesn't look very good. Plus, I haven't successfully set up port forwarding yet, so I am actually considering whether to pay for ProtonVPN's service... To be honest, ProtonVPN's plans and pricing (VPN Plus 2-year plan at 4.99 USD/month) actually seem quite viable...

V2Ray on Cloudflare

After leaving China, I haven't spent much effort or skill points on anti-censorship wall-circumvention tools anymore... However, while watching YouTube last time, I discovered that you can set up a serverless V2Ray server using free Cloudflare Workers, and it even comes with multiple IPs that can be refreshed and changed... I can only say it is truly a blessing...

Edgetunnel​

Edgetunnel from cmliu

Actually, the moment I found this project, 90% of the setup was already done. The remaining part is having a Cloudflare account—though you might not even need one since CF Workers automatically generate a URL like worker_name.User_name.workers.dev for you. However... as someone who has previously set up V2Ray WebSockets over TLS myself, hosting on a custom domain under CF can be considered a standard setup... so none of these should be an issue, unless someone starts completely from scratch with nothing at all, in which case they might really need to put in some effort to get a domain...

Next, just create a free Worker project, paste the code from GitHub into the Worker editor, go to an online UUID generator to get a pleasing UUID put any arbitrary string as a token into the 4th line let userID = '<uuid you like>';, and deploy it.

Then go to the Worker's Settings -> Domains and Routes to configure your domain, or resign yourself to using the workers.dev link (though I only tested that it connects; not sure what might happen if actually used), and visit https://your.domain.or.workers.dev/UUID to see a screen similar to the one below:

Client​

Windows​

Basically V2RayN works. Just import the subscription group, refresh, and you're good to go.

Android​

Unfortunately, V2RayNG does not support group subscription features, so I had to test ClashMeta for Android instead. I installed it directly from GitHub using Obtainium... Detailed configuration methods... too lazy to write them out. Basically anyone who knows how to use V2RayNG will know how to configure it themselves from a subscription URL, just by filling in https://your.domain.or.workers.dev/UUID into the URL field.....

iOS​

No hardware... so not tested. Even friends who have hardware are far away in China, so let's skip testing... too troublesome Updated: Tested singbox app using a colleague's iOS device. It looks pretty good, but you have to comment out 127.0.0.1 in the source code first, and all nodes must be online in order to use it. Not sure if it's due to my bad configuration or what, but overall the user experience was pretty poor... Might need to spend more time looking into it.

MacOS​

Do you think someone who doesn't even have iOS hardware would have MacOS hardware??? (If I really had one, I probably would have used it to install Asahi Linux anyway...)

Reflections​

  • Indeed, being outside of China and lacking the pressure of the GFW makes it really hard to ignite my passion for testing a bunch of things Without the network environment inside China, I can't optimize IPs specifically for Jiangsu...
  • Same as above, so I actually don't know how effective the created nodes really are... can only look at user feedback Based on feedback from friends physically located in China, it's much better than my previous nodes and the speed is fast enough...
  • I used to feel that living in China required spending a bunch of skill points on tunneling tools. Although skill is skill... learning things always brings a sense of achievement, especially when they are easily applied practically. But looking back without absolute necessity, it really is a waste of skill points...
  • Looking at the VPNs sold nowadays—many using the WireGuard protocol while tunnels in China are almost all disguised as WebSocket-based SOCKS servers—I feel quite wistful, especially since I need Wireguard every day to connect back home. Feeling wistful that WireGuard is so easy to set up and extremely efficient... I suppose one can only helplessly accept that one cannot choose where they are born.

entry.title: Hooked on Ansible....
entry.summary: A log of wrestling with Ansible
entry.content:

This article was migrated from the old blog archive.

Originally, I wanted to pull myself together and write some shell scripts... Then halfway through, I thought some steps might be simpler to write using ansible. Once I started writing... I became irretrievably hooked on it....

What is Ansible?

Ansible is an automation tool developed by RedHat. Through Python and SSH, it achieves "one control machine rules them all". It's not like I hadn't tried it before, but back then I just thought Ansible was slow, complicated, and hard to understand.... So I messed around with some beginner stuff and gave up. This time, something suddenly clicked in my head, and as I kept writing, it started covering more and more ground.

Related Tutorials​

Here are some references and videos for beginners who want to try using Ansible:

Documents​

  • Ansible Community Documentation
  • Ansible Community Documentation (CN)
  • Ansible Authoritative Chinese Guide

YouTube Tutorial Videos​

Jay from Learn Linux TV offers lots of useful Linux tutorial videos (though mostly focused on the basics). Besides Ansible, you can also browse his other topic playlists.

Previous Roadblocks​

Previously, I mainly got stuck on two things when using Ansible:

Using Variables / Loops​

Loops in Ansible almost always go hand-in-hand with variables. If you don't know how to define the "{{ }}" Jinja2 variable syntax, you basically can't use loops. An Ansible playbook without loops becomes bloated—the more machines and repetitive tasks you have, the more verbose and sluggish it runs.

Conditionals​

This is also a huge point. Just like with shell script, if you don't know how to use if ..else ..fi to check states, you won't get very far writing a shell script either....

Other Addictive Parts​

include_task, include_roles​

Previously, I already liked Ansible's roles feature—after all, it lets you break down a huge playbook.yml into smaller, easier-to-write roles, reducing the writing burden and enabling reuse. However, roles are static: whatever you write there will definitely be called and executed. When combined with include_task and variable checks, though, you can inspect a node's properties (such as os_family to automatically detect the OS type) and dynamically load the corresponding task.yml. That expands the coverage of a single playbook.yml to almost every machine (especially for someone like me who likes using different distributions for different types of servers/workstations).

Remaining Issues

Still Don't Understand Advanced Usage​

Ansible is a tool that's constantly evolving with tons of people diving deep into it, so there are still quite a few complex conditional checks and loop patterns I don't really understand (yeah... the kind where I don't even understand someone else's example...). So the playbook.yml I'm writing right now still looks pretty rough, and its efficiency isn't optimized to the max, though at least it works.... Then again, my shell script writing level is about the same... so I guess they're six of one, half a dozen of the other...

Beautifying Output​

This one is purely asking for extra trouble... Although you can set display.skipped.host=false in ansible.cfg to hide skipped items and make the output look nicer—or even go further and set display.ok.host=false so nothing shows up except changed items.... Or I saw a trick using callback parameter tweaks so nothing displays unless explicitly defined (kind of like only showing text from echo inside a shell script). Truth be told, I don't really need to spend effort on this anyway, since I have no intention of publishing my Ansible project externally.... Either way, I'm the only one using it, so it doesn't matter if it's ugly—good enough is good enough.

Conclusion

First off, since my Ansible progress has jumped way ahead compared to before, I now have a bunch of notes waiting to be updated into the wiki.... (Procrastination is about to strike...) So for the foreseeable future, I'm going to have plenty of things to do... How exciting~~ (Wait, what?!) I've dug myself a hole... now let's see if I can fill it in later.

Generative AI

I've been quiet for a long time—not only because I've been going to physical therapy continuously trying to relieve the sciatica that has bothered me for ages, but mostly because life has settled into calm, with no urge to tinker with new things.

Suddenly realizing I'm becoming more and more like an idle retiree with nothing to do, yesterday I decided to make work for myself and started testing some things I don't actually need...

Conclusion

Jumping straight to the conclusion: after spending a whole day testing, there were zero worthwhile results, so I deleted everything... Still, let me briefly share my thoughts on what I tried.

Research (!?) Topics

Most of the tests involved multimedia-related services.

Xiaoya Alist​

I admit it—after watching the showcase, I was tempted and wanted to set it up... But I died on Step 1 of Step 1 — creating an Aliyun Drive account... because I don't have a Chinese phone number... So I can only imagine that I probably could have gotten it running...

TubeArchivist​

TubeArchivist is an offline YouTube archiver. Its basic function is subscribing to a YouTube channel and downloading all the videos from that channel for offline viewing...

Moreover, it can integrate and serve those files to emby/plex/jellyfin as library media for playback.

TubeArchivist-Plugin for metadata​

Even though TubeArchivist downloads the actual video files, the filenames are based on YouTube IDs rather than human-readable metadata. So people developed plugins to pull YouTube metadata and convert it for emby/jellyfin so that what you see looks proper.

TubeArchivist-emby​

Because emby doesn't have it implemented as a plugin, you have to attach an external Python service to convert it. I spent an entire morning on it and still couldn't get it working, and I didn't feel like debugging Python code... so I stamped it "Abandoned."

TubeArchivist-JF-Plugin​

Just to make it work, I even went and installed jellyfin, and it succeeded! The gotchas are:

  • After installing the plugin, remember to restart Jellyfin, otherwise the plugin won't initialize.

  • After configuring and saving the plugin settings, remember to restart Jellyfin again, otherwise the connection will keep failing... and it won't be able to update metadata.

IPTV​

Jellyfin​

Since Emby's Live TV feature requires a paid unlock... and I happened to have Jellyfin up because of TubeArchivist, I set my sights on Jellyfin.

In the end, after struggling through a mountain of IPTV prerequisite configs (strictly speaking, still not really sorted out since my EPG program guide was still broken), it still wouldn't play... (the exact same stream link worked in VLC, and even in Emby's IPTV Plugin it played TV channels fine, yet Jellyfin just threw an error and refused to play... so I gave up on it too... and wiped the working TA setup along with it).

Xetve​

This is an IPTV Tuner and Guide aggregator tool, though I never managed to figure it out in the end...

Related Links​

  • IPTV-org
  • XMLTV Source
  • EPG.PW

Emby​

Even though Live TV costs money, there is a free IPTV plugin you can install. Basically, you can watch channels by adding valid m3u links from iptv-org one by one... However, bandwidth can be insufficient, and the picture quality is an unbearable 480p... so giving up is probably the sensible choice...

Conclusion Again...

Even though it failed... at least I spent some time tinkering... I'll see what else I can dig into later...

As mentioned in the previous post, I recently moved and reorganized all the systems and services at home(the Combined Fleet). Besides the hardware focus from the last post, I also want to review the software side(vent and complain).

OS Installation

I used to put quite a few installation scripts on my wiki, but this time I realized a lot of them aren't needed anymore (or don't need to be written like that).

Archlinux​

Ever since Archlinux introduced the archinstall automated install script.. I haven't needed to write my own Archlinux install scripts anymore (of course, if you need to deploy many hosts with specialized configs you still can...). Mainly, Docker is so convenient now that I don't need so many VMs running individual Archlinux hosts, so the ROI of writing automated install scripts has dropped dramatically...

Unifi Network Application​

After fighting with this thing, I still couldn't get it running properly in Docker (just like dnsmasq), so in the end I had to put it on an

Archlinux host. Installing it was pretty simple though—just as mentioned in the last post, you only need to install it from AUR.

However, I later discovered it might be an SSL issue—I gave it an internal domain pointing to it, yet couldn't access the admin UI via that domain and could only connect with https://ip:8443 Confirmed afterward that it wasn't a DN issue; Vaultwarden just had the wrong saved entry so I couldn't log in.... (I repent!)

Windows​

Ever since Windows 10, installing Windows hasn't taken much time or effort anyway. Now, possibly because it's leaning closer to Linux (not sure if that's the reason), Windows's CLI tools have gotten pretty nice too. So nowadays I install apps directly with winget—not because it's cooler, just because apps installed via winget can easily be updated with winget.

# Search for app XXX
winget search XXX

# Install app XXX
winget install XXX

# Uninstall app XXX
winget uninstall XXX

# Update all apps
winget update --all

PhotonOS​

There's really nothing special to configure for this. For version 5.0 that I installed this time, as long as the initial IP setup is fine, at most you just

add the NFS folder to mount in /etc/fstab, remember to install docker-compose (now you can just install it via yum install docker-compose), and run systemctl enable docker.service plus systemctl enable remote-fs.target so the machine starts Docker and mounts the NFS folder automatically on boot.

Docker​

After testing, no matter how I tried, nfs-volume still kept failing on me. So for now I'm sticking to the old-school method: creating Docker volumes locally and using a script to automatically back them up to the NFS folder, which is simpler.

Summary

I think I need to do a major overhaul of the stuff in my wiki, because quite a lot of things aren't used anymore. Going forward, scripts will probably lean toward personal-use tools, and I'll likely spend some time studying Ansible again.

entry.content:

A little while ago I finally finished renovating and moving into my new place. Staying true to the spirit of hardware lifecycle upgrades(chasing shiny new toys), I replaced almost all the networking gear and servers at the new house, so naturally it's time to jot down some notes on the hardware swaps and setup changes.

Hardware Overview

  • ASUS TS110-E14

    • This is now my main ESXi Server, currently running the following VMs:

      • FreeBSD 14-release x1: Gateway + Firewall

      • Archlinux x1: DHCPd + DNS + UniFi Network Application

      • PhotonOS 5 x3: Docker hosts for Containers

      • XigmaNAS 13 With PCI passthrough x2: Server Backup and Temp

  • HPE MicroServer Gen8

    • XigmaNAS 13: Main NAS for Media Center

  • UniFi Switch Enterprise 8 PoE

    • Main Switch

  • Access Point U6 In-Wall

  • Access Point U6 Pro (in transit)

Detailed Notes

UniFi Series​

Honestly, the main motivation here was just showing off...

I figured I'd upgrade my new home's IT infrastructure to prosumer/semi-enterprise grade, and being able to push settings to APs from a single central controller seemed much more convenient. Plus I got burned by the TP-Link Deco X75 I bought for my parents' place earlier—a pricey Mesh AP that didn't even have a whitelist mode for MAC Address filtering...

Originally I thought the apartment wasn't big so a single U6 In-Wall would cover everything, but unfortunately the placement wasn't great and the signal behind the TV wall ended up weak.

So I bought a U6 Pro to fill in the dead zone.

HPE MicroServer Gen8​

This is an older box—I used to have two of them, but my parents' ASUS Server died (after ~10 years, it definitely earned its keep), so I had to move one back there to serve as their NAS. The remaining one got a 10GbE NIC + 16TB HDD x4 upgrade, turning it into a 48TB usable raidz1 NAS.

ASUS TS110-E14​

No surprises here—this is the ESXi Server, though setting up the foundational network environment was still quite a headache.

FreeBSD 14 Gateway​

Sticking with old habits, I still went with the tried-and-true FreeBSD + pf + ipfw for the gateway.

Network Architecture​

Initially I wanted to put everything on a single Class C subnet to keep things simple (which meant no DMZ isolation, though DMZ was basically half-baked in my hands anyway). Turns out I hit a NAT Loopback issue where internal hosts couldn't access my external-facing services, so I had to revert back to the original WAN+LAN+DMZ layout—after tweaking the pf rules, I fixed it by referring to this guide:

# Nat Loopback
no nat on $int_if proto tcp from $int_if to $int_net
rdr on $int_if proto tcp from $int_net to $ext_ip port { 25, 165, 993 } -> 192.168.0.2
nat on $int_if proto tcp from $int_net to 192.168.0.2 port { 25, 165, 993 } -> $int_if

So in the end, I still managed to consolidate everything back onto a single Class C subnet.

Archlinux Dnsmasq + UniFi​

This turned out to be part of the big landmine of this build. My original plan was to just spin up both dnsmasq and UniFi Network Application in Docker containers and call it a day, and well...

Dnsmasq​

It ran in Docker, sure, but because of IP subnetting and me not digging carefully into network mapping, the service appeared to be up while none of the clients could actually get DHCP or DNS working properly. After fighting with it forever, moving dnsmasq onto a standalone VM made everything work immediately without changing a single thing...

UniFi Network Application​

This one was even more infuriating. Either the MongoDB version specified in the docs threw issues, or once MongoDB was sorted out, the controller refused to serve the web UI properly due to Java version mismatches... After wading through walls of documentation, I discovered that on Archlinux with yay installed, all you need is:

yay -S unifi

And then just make sure the JRE version is 17... One single command took care of everything...

XigmaNAS​

Given the storage needs of the Docker backend and system backups, I mounted a ZFS Mirror NAS via NFS to the various servers for basic backups. Later on, I'll pair it with a self-hosted Git server for overall internal project management.

Also, on my parents' old server I used to attach an HDD directly in ESXi as a TEMP drive for BT downloads and overflow storage, and during this migration I suffered horribly because certain VMs refused to boot without that HDD attached.

So this time I mounted the Temp HDD inside XigmaNAS and exported it over NFS instead.

Pain Points Along the Way

XigmaNAS Refusing to Mount the Temp Drive​

For whatever reason, my existing XigmaNAS VM just wouldn't add the Temp drive, so in the end I had to spin up an extra VM with dedicated PCI Passthrough hardware running a separate XigmaNAS instance solely for exporting Temp storage.

UniFi Series​

As mentioned earlier, the cursed UniFi-Network-Application wouldn't behave properly in Docker... plus Dnsmasq didn't play nice either, so I ended up spinning up an extra VM.

Poor WiFi AP Placement​

My brain must have been eaten by something during the interior design phase, because the U6 In-Wall ended up in a terrible spot—facing away from two bedrooms and two bathrooms, leaving weak signal in all of them... So I had to add a U6 Pro, kicking off the UniFi asexual reproduction cycle ahead of schedule...

Conclusion

Living in a new home is wonderful, though the moving process itself is not... Getting new servers and redesigning the architecture is fun(?), whereas emergency-rescuing dying hardware and migrating mountains of data is definitely not...

I'll update the wiki with the detailed config changes later on.

Due to unknown reasons(an 80% chance my kids did it), the screen on my company-issued laptop completely died, leaving me living with an external monitor only for quite a while...

With the help of our partner-in-crime(kind-hearted) IT guy, I got another laptop replacement..

Naturally, I had to do some Fine Tune(illegal modification)..

Machine Introduction

I guess I got lucky this time—not only is this batch not Lenovo(the evil CCP brand), it was originally meant for an ME, so they gave me a Dell Precision 3561.

It turned out to be a blessing in disguise with an overall spec bump: CPU from 11th gen i5 to 11th gen i7 (okay, I know both are CPUs from several generations ago) RAM from 16GB to 32GB (this actually makes a real difference... since I like running all sorts of random stuff) GPU from Intel Iris@Xe to Nvidia T600 Laptop (alright, a bit faster)

Machine Setup

Basically this is still a company laptop, so I can't modify it too drastically (though the kind IT guy did give me Admin privileges so I could do some tuning first).

Basic​

Since it's a company machine, it naturally runs Windows 11 pro. When I got it, the company's work software was already pre-installed (what? You thought my job only needed a browser? How could that be, I still need Office too!), so I just used Winget to install the following:

  • Open-shell - Okay, this isn't the most important thing, I just hate the post-Win10 Start menu so I installed it.

  • VirtualBox - This is actually one of the core pieces; with vbox I can pretty much do my own thing.

  • WSL - This is also quite important, though I ran into some issues this time.

VitrualBox​

This is really simple—just installing Arch Linux inside a VM...

WSL​

Dilemma​

This Windows installation is super weird—I actually couldn't install the new version of WSL from anywhere... it kept throwing error code 0x80070490. Running wsl --update just told me element not found.... The price of that is... WSL Distros can't properly use systemd (which is absurd, since one of Windows 11's selling points is built-in systemd support in the new WSL).

Workaround and Result​

I basically switched to ArchWSL2 from Sileshn because that version is actively maintained... As for the systemd issue, the only reason I actually needed systemd inside WSL was for systemd-resolved.service for Wireguard, so switching resolvconf to oopenresolv solved it.

Little Discovery​

I really love the default customized zsh theme in Manjaro KDE. Previously I always copied the customization files directly from /usr/share/zsh/, until I recently discovered that AUR actually has manjaro-zsh-config. After installing it, you just need to make sure ~/.zshrc has the right contents. The only minor downside is that its console color is Manjaro green instead of Arch blue.

Conclusion and Future Plans

Conclusion? Honestly, that's about it—once everything is set up, just be good and go to work.... The next step is figuring out how to squeeze a bit more GPU performance out for WSL or the VM...

Amazed by Archinstall, I'm considering switching from Manjaro to Archlinux. Let's start with my WSL and a VM in VirtualBox...

ArchWSL

Github Project​

  • Link - GitHub - yuk7/ArchWSL

  • Online Manual - How to Setup | ArchWSL official documentation

Notes​

  • You need to initialize archlinux-keyring first to avoid issues:

    [root@wsl]$ pacman-key --init
    [root@wsl]$ pacman-key --populate
    [root@wsl]$ pacman -Sy archlinux-keyring
    [root@wsl]$ pacman -Syyu

  • You need to create a regular user account (otherwise some GUI apps will have issues):

    # 定義wheel群組的User都可以sudo
    [root@wsl]$ echo "%wheel ALL=(ALL) ALL" > /etc/sudoers.d/wheel
    # 建立一個{username}帳號,並且屬於wheel群組
    [root@wsl]$ useradd -m -G wheel -s /bin/bash `{username}`

  • You need to set {username} as the default user—this operation must be done outside WSL:

    [User@Windows]$ Arch.exe config --default-user `{username}`

Archlinux Guest in Virtualbox

Install​

Basically you just boot from the ISO, pick your options in archinstall, and install directly. From testing it myself, if you need a desktop you can just choose its desktop profile. Looking at my own choice of KDE:

  • It installs both Xorg & Wayland by default, and you can choose between them at the SDDM login screen.

    • Currently Wayland support still isn't great—even ArchWiki recommends sticking with Xorg for now.

Essential Packages​

Recommended essential packages are as follows:

Pkg NameDescription
gitAside from regular Git usage, installing AUR packages before yay is set up (including installing yay itself) relies on it.
base-develThis is actually a package group containing compilers and related tools, needed if you compile packages yourself.
virtualbox-guest-utilsVirtualBox guest tools including special drivers, equivalent to VMware Tools.
yayAnyone using an Arch-based distro knows what this is. Manjaro lets you install it directly with pacman, while on Arch you have to install it using the method below.

How to Install yay (under Archlinux)​

# 不能用root
[user@archlinux]$ git clone https://aur.archlinux.org/yay-git.git
[user@archlinux]$ cd yay-git
[user@archlinux]$ makepkg -si

Notes​

  • systemd services need to be enabled manually:

    • systemd-resolved.service

      • This is the systemd version of resolvconf, mainly needed by wireguard.

      • systemctl enable --now systemd-resolved.service

    • vboxservice.service

      • This automatically loads components from virtualbox-guest-utils.

      • systemctl enable --now vboxservice.service

Conclusion

From what I've seen so far, as long as you copy over some customization configs from Manjaro (or another distro you like, such as zsh-theme-powerlevel10k settings), Archlinux won't look plain at all.

Installation has also become super easy. In daily use it's Arch-based, pretty much no different (compared to Manjaro).

I'll probably need to observe it for a while longer before making a clearer comparison of pros and cons.
